guard: a recursive delete refuses any target that is not a strict child of the root it was minted under, and a control socket path over sun_path is refused by name rather than by a bare EINVAL
why: THE GUARD IS GRADED THROUGH THE ASSERTION, NOT THROUGH A DELETE, and that is deliberate rather
than timid. The incident this file exists for was a cleanup that deleted the PARENT of its own
mkdtemp — on a host where tmpdir() is /tmp, that took an orchestrator's relay socket and
fourteen seats' control sockets, and stopped only on a root-owned EPERM. A fixture that proved
the fix by performing the delete would reproduce the outage to demonstrate that the outage is
fixed. The containment DECISION lives in assertContainedIn, so every mutation below disarms a
real branch of the real guard and every cell reads a refusal that did not happen — with no
traversing path ever reaching rmSync.
NO MUTATION HERE TOUCHES A PATH ANY SUITE LATER DELETES, MOVES OR WRITES INTO. The mutants
change comparison logic only; none changes what a path RESOLVES to, which is the class that
caused the incident and must not be re-triggered to test the fix for it.
THE THIRD MUTATION IS THE ONE THAT LOOKS HARMLESS. Swapping physical() for resolve() leaves a
containment check that still refuses '..' and still refuses the root itself, so two of the three
Part A cells stay green. Only the symlink cell moves. A lexical prefix compare is satisfied by a
symlink pointing anywhere, so that single cell is the whole difference between 'contained' and
'contained unless someone made a link', and without it the canonicalization could be dropped in a
tidying commit with every other cell still green.
PART B IS GRADED ON THE MESSAGE, NOT ON THE THROW. EINVAL already fails; what was missing was a
failure that names the path, its length and the limit. The cell asserts all three, so a refusal
that regressed to a bare throw would redden it.
